theme: How good and pleasant when brothers dwell in unity
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 133. It is three verses long. It is a Song of Ascents, sung by pilgrims on their way to Jerusalem. Read it slowly twice and picture the two images: oil and dew.
settingTheScene: Psalm 133 is a psalm of David and belongs to the pilgrim songs. When Israelite families came together from all over the land for the festivals in Jerusalem, they experienced the unity of the people of God. In the context of 1 Corinthians, a church torn by factions, this psalm is a picture of what Paul longed to see. Unity is not an optional extra but a gift and a command.
observation: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!” (v. 1).
“It is like the precious oil on the head” (v. 2).
“Running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron” (v. 2).
“Running down on the collar of his robes!” (v. 2).
“It is like the dew of Hermon” (v. 3).
“Which falls on the mountains of Zion” (v. 3).
“For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore” (v. 3).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with an exclamation: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!” The words “good” and “pleasant” mean something that is both right and delightful. We often think of unity as duty. The psalm says it is a delight. The word translated “brothers” includes the whole family of God. The unity described is among those who “dwell together,” sharing life.

Then two pictures. First, precious oil poured on the head of Aaron the high priest at his consecration (Exodus 29:7, Leviticus 8:12). It ran down on the beard and the collar of his robes. Oil was abundant, fragrant, and set apart for holy use. Unity is like holy oil that flows down from the head over the whole body. It is a lavish, overflowing gift. For Christians, the Head is Christ, and the Spirit he sends is poured out on the whole body. The oil of anointing reaches to the collar and beyond: to every member.

The second picture is dew from Mount Hermon, the tallest mountain in the region, covered in snow and heavy with moisture. In the dry summers, dew was life for the crops. The dew of Hermon falls on the mountains of Zion, which are much farther south and drier. The picture is of refreshment coming down from above to fertilize a dry land. Unity is life-giving.

“For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore.” Notice that the blessing is “commanded.” God designates unity as the place where he gives life. In Christ’s prayer in John 17, he asked that his followers be one, so that the world may believe. And Paul calls the Corinthians to the same unity: “that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you.”

We should not romanticize unity. It requires forgiveness, patience, and humility. It does not mean agreeing on everything, but sharing the same Lord, the same gospel, and the same Spirit. Ephesians 4:3 says to be “eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” The unity is already ours in Christ; our job is to guard and display it.
connection: Exodus 29:7 and Leviticus 8:12 describe the anointing of Aaron. Deuteronomy 33:28 mentions dew. John 17:20-23 is Jesus’ prayer for unity. Ephesians 4:1-6 urges us to maintain unity. Colossians 3:12-15 describes the bond of perfect harmony. Philippians 2:1-4 calls for being of one mind. Acts 2:42-47 and 4:32 describe the early church’s unity. 1 Corinthians 1:10 and 12:12-26 treat unity in Corinth. Romans 15:5-6 prays for harmony. Hebrews 13:1 says let brotherly love continue.
application:
Think of a fellow believer you are at odds with. Take a step to be reconciled.

Pray for the unity of your church by name: elders, volunteers, and members.

Thank God for a time when you tasted unity with others, and ask for more.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the unity of his people.
Ask him to pour out his Spirit like precious oil on your church.
Pray for peace in a specific relationship.
